summary: Mortals return to dust and wither like grass before the eternal God; the psalm asks for a wise heart, mercy and lasting work.

context.title: A prayer of Moses
paragraphs: Psalm 90 opens the fourth book of the Psalter, and its heading calls it a prayer of Moses, the man of God. [c1] The same title is given to Moses in Deut 33:1. [c2] Many modern commentators doubt that Moses wrote it, noting its closeness to Deuteronomy and an outlook that seems to reach beyond his age. [c3]

The selection leaves out the psalm’s middle verses, which speak of a life spent under God’s anger at sin. [c4] It keeps the contrast between God, for whom a thousand years are like yesterday, and mortals who return to dust and pass like grass. [c5] The second letter of Peter takes up the saying about a thousand years. [c6]

In Palestine some grasses shoot up lushly in spring and are soon scorched and gone, which gives the image its force. [c7] The closing prayer asks God for a morning of mercy after a night of trouble, and to establish the work of our hands, a phrase frequent in Deuteronomy. [c8][c9]

translationNotes.summary: Dakka means what is crushed small; the psalm echoes Genesis 3:19 in words of its own.
translationNotes.body: Dakka properly means something beaten or crushed very fine, and hence dust. [c10] The Cambridge Bible renders it pulverisation, the dissolving of the body into its elements. [c11] The verse plainly recalls Gen 3:19, where the man taken from the ground is told he will return to dust, though the psalmist chooses different words. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: The prayer’s “Return” uses the verb of verse 3, where God bids mortals return to dust.
translationNotes.body: Verse 13 opens with the verb shuv, the same verb God uses in verse 3 when he tells mortals to return to the dust. [c13] Keil and Delitzsch hear the prayer of Moses in Exod 32:12 and read it as a plea that God turn from his anger. [c14] The Cambridge Bible adds that Scripture speaks of God relenting in human terms, without implying that he changes his purpose. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: Hebrew asks for “a heart of wisdom”, brought in like a harvest, once our days are rightly counted.
translationNotes.body: Literally the line asks God to make us know how to count our days, so that we may bring in a heart of wisdom. [c16] The verb for bringing in was used of garnering the harvest. [c17] The petition follows from the fear of God in verse 11, which is the beginning of wisdom. [c18] Ellicott reads the verse differently, with God rather than man as the one who reckons the days. [c19]

translationNotes.summary: No‘am means pleasantness, a word that joins beauty and kindly favour, much like the Greek charis.
translationNotes.body: No‘am properly means pleasantness, and from there beauty or grace. [c20] Ellicott compares the Greek charis and the English grace, which likewise join beauty and favour. [c21] The Septuagint renders it splendour. [c22] The psalm closes by asking that the gracious kindliness of the Lord rest on his people and make their ordinary daily work endure. [c23]

claims.text: Psalm 90 begins Book IV of the Psalter (Psalms 90-106), and its title ascribes it to Moses, the man of God.
“Man of God” is a title of honour applied to Moses in Deut 33:1.
Commentators such as the Cambridge Bible and Ellicott doubt Mosaic authorship, pointing to the psalm’s Deuteronomic language and a retrospect wider than was possible to Moses.
Ps 90:7-11, omitted from the selection, describe life spent under the cloud of God’s wrath for sin.
Ps 90:3-6 contrasts God, to whom a thousand years are as yesterday, with mortals whom God returns to dust and who pass like grass.
2 Pet 3:8 takes up the saying of Ps 90:4 about a thousand years and a day.
Some grasses of the Jordan valley shoot up with great luxuriance in early spring and are quickly scorched and burnt up.
The prayer for satisfaction “in the morning” (Ps 90:14) implies that it has been night, a time of trouble, for Israel.
“The work of our hands” (Ps 90:17) is a phrase characteristic of Deuteronomy, where it occurs seven times.
Dakka means properly anything beaten or broken small or very fine, and hence dust.
The Cambridge Bible explains dakka as literally pulverisation, implying the dissolution of the body into its elements.
Ps 90:3 plainly refers to Gen 3:19, though the psalmist uses different words.
Ps 90:3 and Ps 90:13 both use the verb שׁוּב: God bids mortals return (to dust), and the psalmist bids God turn.
Keil and Delitzsch read Ps 90:13 in the language of Moses’ prayer in Exod 32:12, as a plea for the turning away of God’s anger.
The Cambridge Bible notes that God’s relenting is spoken of after the manner of men, not implying that he can regret his course of action.
Ps 90:12 literally reads “to number our days make us know, and we will bring a heart of wisdom”.
The verb in “bring a heart of wisdom” is used of garnering in the harvest.
The Cambridge Bible links the petition of Ps 90:12 to the fear of God in Ps 90:11, which is the beginning of wisdom.
Ellicott argues that the natural reading makes God, not man, the reckoner of the days in Ps 90:12.
No‘am means properly pleasantness, then beauty, splendour or grace.
Ellicott compares no‘am with Greek χάρις and English “grace”, which combine the ideas of beauty and favour.
The Septuagint renders no‘am in Ps 90:17 as λαμπρότης, splendour.
The Cambridge Bible explains the beauty of the Lord as his gracious kindliness, and the work of our hands as all the ordinary undertakings of daily life.
